title: At What Age Should My Teenager Transition to Adolescent Gynecology Services?
excerpt: ACOG suggests a first gynecology visit between ages 13 and 15. Learn what to expect and when to go sooner.
blocks: Parents in Portland and Beaverton often ask when their teen should start gynecology care. The answer is simpler than many people expect.

The American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG) generally recommends a first gynecology visit between ages 13 and 15. This visit is about more than a physical exam. Most first visits do not include an internal pelvic exam.
The first visit is a chance to:
Build trust in a comfortable, non-judgmental space where your teen can talk about their health.
Learn about puberty, periods and body development, and clear up myths and peer misinformation.
Talk about healthy habits, body image and reproductive health in a private setting.
Consider an earlier visit if you notice:
Period problems, such as very heavy or painful periods, or no period by age 15.
Pelvic pain, unusual discharge or hormone changes.
Questions about sexual health, including sexual activity, birth control or STI prevention.

title: Surviving the 2026 Spring Allergy Surge: A Guide for Beaverton Parents
excerpt: An early, strong pollen season is expected. Learn how to tell a cold from allergies and how to manage symptoms.
blocks: Oregon springs are lovely, but the 2026 pollen forecast for the Portland area points to an earlier and stronger season than usual. For families near our Beaverton clinic on SW Nimbus Ave, this can mean cold-like symptoms that last a long time.
Is it a cold or spring allergies?
Parents often tell our pediatric team they cannot tell if a child has a lingering virus or seasonal allergies. These signs point to allergies:
Rubbing the nose upward often. This is called the “allergic salute.”
Itchy, watery or red eyes without thick discharge.
Sneezing that keeps going, especially after outdoor play at places like Greenway Park or Tualatin Hills.
Tree pollen is expected to stay high for several weeks, so we suggest a proactive plan:
Check Beaverton pollen counts and limit outdoor play during peak morning hours.
Make an after-school routine: change clothes and wash hands and face right after your child comes home from school or daycare.
If your child has known allergies, talk with our clinicians about starting preventive treatment before symptoms peak.
Compassionate, expert care at Nimbus Ave

Our Beaverton office can help with everything from mild hay fever to asthma triggers in the environment. We aim to give patient-centered care so children can breathe easily and enjoy the Oregon spring.

title: Newborn Vaccines: What Parents Should Know in the First Weeks of Life
excerpt: Why newborns need vaccines, which ones come first, what side effects to expect, and how we guide you.
blocks: Do newborns really need vaccines if they already have immunity?
Babies get some temporary antibody protection from the parent during pregnancy. This protection fades, so vaccines help babies build their own immunity.
What vaccines do newborns receive first?
The first vaccine is given soon after birth. Other routine vaccines follow in the first months, based on the current schedule. Your provider will guide you through it.
Why are vaccines given so early in life?
Many vaccine-preventable illnesses are most dangerous for young infants. Early vaccines:
Protect babies during the most vulnerable months.
Help prevent severe disease and complications.
Reduce spread within families and communities.
Vaccines are studied and monitored, and the doses are made for infants. Serious reactions are very rare. Your provider can talk with you about risks, benefits and what to expect.
What side effects should parents expect?
Most babies have little or no reaction. Mild, short effects can happen:
Soreness or redness where the shot was given
Extra sleepiness for a short time
There is a lot of vaccine misinformation online
Vaccine content online is often wrong, so your pediatric provider is a key source of trusted information. We welcome your vaccine questions and never rush you.
How do you know which vaccines your baby actually needs?
You do not have to track the schedule alone. Our providers follow current guidelines and review your baby's immunizations at every well-baby visit.
Why newborn and infant vaccines are so important for your family
Vaccines protect your newborn and the people around them:
Other infants and medically fragile children in the community
Pediatric care you can trust for your newborn

title: Is Strep Throat Contagious? How to Know for Sure and When to Get Tested in Portland
excerpt: Yes, strep throat is contagious. Learn how long, how to tell it from a virus, and when to get a test.
blocks: A sore throat that appears suddenly at home or school makes many parents ask: is strep throat contagious? Our teams see many worried families, so here are clear answers.
Yes. Strep throat is caused by group A Streptococcus and spreads from person to person:
By sharing drinks, utensils, food or toothbrushes
By touching contaminated surfaces and then the mouth or nose
This is why strep is common in schools, daycares and busy households.
How long is strep throat contagious?
Contagious for 24 hours after the first antibiotic dose
Untreated strep can stay contagious for several days or longer, so even a mildly ill child can spread it.
Can you spread strep throat before you know you have it?
Yes. People can spread strep before they notice symptoms, especially in the early stages. This is why several people in one home often get sick within a week.
How can you tell if a sore throat is actually strep?
Symptoms alone cannot confirm strep. Viral illnesses look similar but do not need antibiotics. These signs may suggest strep, but none prove it:
White patches or streaks on the tonsils
Swollen lymph nodes in the neck
Headache or stomach pain, especially in children
How do you know for sure if you have strep throat?
Testing is the only reliable way. We use a throat swab and a rapid strep test, and sometimes send a throat culture to a lab. Testing matters because:
Antibiotics only work against bacterial infections.
Antibiotics will not help a viral sore throat.
Antibiotics you do not need cause side effects and add to antibiotic resistance.
When should you get tested for strep?
Get tested for a sore throat with:
Swollen or tender neck lymph nodes
Recent close contact with someone who has strep
A fast start or pain worse than a typical cold
Children, teens and families with several sick members should be seen early.
How quickly can you stop spreading strep throat?

Most people stop being contagious about 24 hours after starting antibiotics. Keep children home from school or daycare until they have taken antibiotics for a full day and their fever is gone. This protects classmates, teachers and coworkers.
Why confirming strep matters for your health

A quick, correct diagnosis can shorten symptoms, shorten the contagious period and lower the risk of problems like ear and sinus infections and more serious inflammatory conditions. Testing also avoids unneeded medicine when a virus is the cause.

title: Strep Throat: Symptoms, Treatment, and When to See a Doctor in the Portland Area

Strep throat is a bacterial infection of the throat and tonsils caused by group A Streptococcus. It is most common in school-age children, but adults can get it too. Unlike many viral sore throats, it usually needs prescription antibiotics.
Swollen lymph nodes in the neck
Headache or stomach pain, especially in children
A cough, runny nose and hoarseness are less common with strep and more typical of a virus.
Close contact with an infected person
Children in schools and daycares are at higher risk.

A sore throat alone cannot confirm strep. Providers use an exam plus a rapid strep test or throat culture. Antibiotics do not help viral sore throats, and they can add side effects and antibiotic resistance.
Over-the-counter pain or fever relief when right for you
Most people feel better within 24 to 48 hours of starting antibiotics. Always finish the full prescription.
Early treatment shortens the illness, reduces spread and helps prevent problems such as ear or sinus infections and more serious inflammatory conditions. Children's symptoms can get worse quickly.
Sore throat with fever and no cough
Trouble swallowing or opening the mouth
Swollen neck glands with a lot of throat pain
Repeated sore throats in a short time
Infants, young children and people with long-term conditions should be seen sooner.

title: 5 Questions to Ask at a Well-Child Exam
excerpt: Make the most of your child's yearly checkup with these five questions for your pediatrician.
blocks: Well-child exams help protect and support your child's health. We recommend at least one every year to check growth and development, keep vaccines up to date and address health concerns. Each visit is also a chance to ask questions.
Sellwood Medical Clinic has four metro Portland-area locations and offers these yearly exams as part of our pediatric care. Here are five questions to bring to your next visit.
1. Is my child's development on track?
Your pediatrician tracks development over time. Ask if your child is growing at a healthy rate, building skills on schedule, or needs a closer look.
2. Is my child up to date on vaccinations?

Vaccines protect against serious illness. Children should get a flu shot every year starting at six months, because young children can get very sick from influenza. Infants are also recommended to get an RSV antibody injection. Ask about upcoming vaccines. Flu, COVID-19 and RSV vaccines can also be scheduled at other times.
3. Is a change or symptom I've noticed cause for alarm?
Parents often worry about unusual changes, especially new parents. Ask if what you see is normal or needs more checking. We may suggest tests or treatment if needed.

A balanced diet helps your child grow. Treats are fine in small amounts, but children need enough nutrients and calories. Ask for general guidance, tips to get your child to eat healthy foods, and whether supplements are right if there is a risk of a deficiency.
5. How can I support my child's wellness moving forward?

Pediatricians can suggest habits and routines that fit your child's needs. They can also tell you when the next checkup should be. Get answers from professionals instead of relying only on web searches.

title: Understanding the Dangers of Untreated Strep Throat
excerpt: Strep throat is very treatable, but without treatment it can lead to serious problems. Here is what to watch for.
blocks: Strep throat is a common, highly contagious infection caused by group A Streptococcus.
Thankfully, strep throat is very treatable when it's addressed early.

It is most common in children ages 5 to 15. Risk factors include crowded indoor spaces, smoke or polluted air, and a weak immune system. It spreads through droplets in the air and on surfaces, such as shared drinking cups.
Symptoms often begin with a sudden sore throat and may include:
Fever, often highest around day two
A cough makes a viral infection more likely than strep.
What happens if strep throat is untreated
Untreated strep can cause serious problems, including:
Abscesses in the neck or tonsils
Rheumatic fever, which can harm the heart and cause stroke
Scarlet fever, which causes a rash
Some children may develop PANDAS, a condition linked to strep that can cause tics or worse OCD symptoms.

Early treatment is the best way to prevent problems. A throat culture at a same-day visit can diagnose strep. Treatment is a course of antibiotics, taken as prescribed. Strep becomes much less contagious within 24 to 48 hours of starting antibiotics. Untreated strep can stay contagious for up to three weeks.

title: The Importance of Getting Your Flu Shot Early
excerpt: When you get your flu shot matters. Learn how it works and why late October is a good target.
blocks: Flu symptoms range from aches and fever to congestion and tiredness, and severe cases may need hospital care. Yearly flu shots in the US prevent millions of illnesses and medical visits and thousands of deaths, and timing affects how much benefit you get.
Sellwood Medical Clinic has four metro Portland-area locations and offers flu shots in the clinic and through drive-thru service.

The vaccine shows your immune system a harmless form of flu strains, so your body builds antibodies. Most US shots cover four flu viruses, chosen based on which strains are expected to spread that year. Higher-dose shots for adults 65 and older give a stronger response.
Why you should get your flu shot (relatively) early

Waiting until flu season starts is not ideal, because your body needs about two weeks after the shot to build full protection. Try to get vaccinated by late October. A shot in July or August may not last through the end of flu season.
Children aged six months to eight years may need two doses at least four weeks apart, so they may need to start earlier.
A well-timed shot has several benefits:
Protection is strongest when viruses in your community peak.
Recovery is shorter if you do get the flu.
Your risk of needing medical care for flu drops by about 40 to 60 percent.
Your risk of severe illness needing the hospital drops by up to 59 percent.
You are less likely to pass the virus to others.
Only about 49 percent of Americans get a flu shot each year. Higher vaccination rates would greatly reduce flu illness and deaths. Early vaccination also gives you peace of mind.

title: 6 Mental Health Challenges Teens Can Experience
excerpt: Anxiety, stress, low mood, ADHD, body image and sleep problems: what to know and how to find support.
blocks: Many young people who need mental health support do not get it. Reading this article is a positive first step. Sellwood Medical Clinic has three metro Portland-area locations and offers pediatric care for teens.

Body changes, social pressure and school demands can fuel teen anxiety. For about 8 percent of young people, worry becomes strong and constant enough to be an anxiety disorder, often with physical symptoms.

Stress is common in teen life because of college planning, busy schedules, new duties and relationships. It is more tied to events than anxiety, but stress that is not managed, or that comes on suddenly, can raise blood pressure and lead to anxiety over time.

Low moods can come from hormone changes or bullying. Severe or long-lasting symptoms may mean a depressive disorder that needs treatment. About one in five teens has major depression, which can also show up as alcohol use, angry outbursts or self-harm.

ADHD is a neurological condition, or a neurodivergent brain type. If it is not treated, it can cause trouble with attention and sitting still, along with sensitivity to rejection. Girls with ADHD often keep thinking about social rejection.
5. Poor body image and disordered eating

Social media, narrow beauty standards and a parent's own body dissatisfaction can all play a part. Self-consciousness may lead to unhealthy habits such as disordered eating or too much exercise. Common eating disorders in teens include:

Most mental health challenges can disrupt sleep, and many teens get less than the 8 to 10 hours they need each night. Health conditions such as asthma and circadian rhythm sleep disorders can also make good sleep harder. Poor sleep is linked to daytime grogginess, irritability, poor focus and tiredness.

Support can include therapy, stress management, medication when right, enjoyable hobbies, a healthy diet and better sleep habits. We are a safe space and can help find hidden causes, such as nutrient shortages and asthma, that may add to mental health problems.
If you notice changes in your teen's mood or behavior, call your nearest clinic or book an appointment online. A teen with signs of suicidal thoughts needs care right away.

title: Back-to-School Prep: How to Set Your Child Up for Success
excerpt: Five simple ways to get your child ready for a new school year, from checkups to bedtime routines.
blocks: Getting ready for a new school year helps children succeed, whether they are starting school for the first time or going back. Our pediatricians can advise your family on school and social readiness.
5 ways to prepare your child for a new school year
Some children find school hard. Here are five practical tips from our pediatricians.
A yearly checkup lets us look at your child's physical and emotional health before school starts. We can address concerns that could affect learning and give resources to the school if needed.
Start adjusting sleep a few weeks before school begins by setting regular bedtime and wake-up times. Good sleep helps prevent mood problems and behavior challenges.
Breakfasts rich in protein, fiber and whole grains support energy and focus. Avoid added sugar, and keep fruits and vegetables ready for after-school snacks.
Open houses and other school events help you stay involved, meet teachers and classmates, understand schoolwork and support the school community.
5. Stay up to date on vaccinations

Keeping your child current on recommended vaccines, including yearly flu shots, helps prevent illness and missed school days. It also lowers the spread of contagious disease to classmates and teachers. If you are not sure what your child needs, schedule an appointment.
